newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds end higher amid fears of shortage.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds end higher amid fears of shortage.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed higher on Thursday with demand up for most bonds amid fears of a shortage of CPI-linked bonds, traders said.
Indices:
* Government bonds general: +0.07 pct to 109.31
* CPI-linked government bonds: +0.1 pct to 108.97
* Unlinked government bonds: +0.06 pct to 109.63
* Dollar-linked government bonds: -0.04 pct to 111.43
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.03 pct to 107.67
Volume including Makams was a moderate 178 million shekels.
"Demand continued for all kinds of bonds today," said Ilan Doron of Solid Financial Markets.

"Demand for CPI-linked bonds continues despite the fact that their yields have broken the four percent psychological barrier. We expect yields of these bonds to continue to fall in the coming months towards 3.7 percent," he said.
Doron explained that demand was up for CPI-linked bonds because of tighter supply expected in coming months.
"We don't expect big government debt issues because there is no real big growth in the budget deficit and bond redemptions are higher than the issues," he said.

Tiki Hadad, of IBI Investment House, said demand for CPI-linked bonds was up because the central bank announced on Thursday that next week it would not issue any CPI-linked bonds, but only unlinked bonds for a total of 150 million shekels.

"I'm not sure what the reasons are. But what is certain is that at this rate there won't be enough CPI-linked bonds to meet demand. There are expected to be 3.5 billion shekels worth of total bond redemptions in July, against new issues of only 1.4 billion shekels, which explains the big demand for bonds," Hadad said.
"The statement of the new finance minister, Yaacov Neeman, that he would not increase the budget deficit, favourably influenced the bond market," said Eyal Segal of United Mizrahi Bank.

Neeman said on Wednesday he intended to stick to budget deficit targets. But he did not say where he might cut the budget to ensure deficit targets set by law -- 2.8 percent of GDP this year, 2.4 percent in 1998 and 1.2 percent within five years -- are met.

Demand for unlinked bonds was up as well on Thursday. Doron said traders were looking to buy them because inflation was not expected to increase and interest rates were not expected to fall despite the rise of the dollar against the shekel.

After the government instituted changes in the exchange rate mechanism and the Bank of Israel slashed interest rates on June 18, the shekel fell sharply against the dollar. After winning back some of its losses, the shekel has generally been trading lower in the last week.
The rise of the dollar against the shekel had prompted fears of a boost in inflation.
Prices of dollar-linked bonds fell on the weakening of the dollar against the shekel on Thursday, traders said.
The shekel rose sharply against the dollar on Thursday. The representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.5520 shekels against 3.5690 on Wednesday.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
($1 = 3.55 shekels)
